summary: Addresses how to manage RBridge nicknames in multilevel TRILL. In the described approach, area border RBridges use a single nickname in both Level 1 and Level 2. RBridges in Level 2 must have unique nicknames, but RBridges in different Level 1 areas may reuse the same ones.

eli5.summary: Each town can reuse the same house numbers as long as the big city uses unique names.

questions: single nickname for area border rbridge
what is a designated border rbridge
what is an area border rbridge
subtitle: How border switches in multilevel TRILL can use one nickname in both areas and let areas reuse nicknames.

tldr.problem: In a multilevel TRILL network, every switch needs a nickname, and managing nicknames across many areas is a major issue.
tldr.mechanism: An area border RBridge uses one nickname in both Level 1 and Level 2. Level 2 nicknames must be unique, but different Level 1 areas may reuse the same nicknames, and border RBridges rewrite ingress and egress nicknames as packets cross levels.
tldr.outcome: Each Level 1 area is identified by the set of its border RBridge nicknames, which allows nickname reuse inside areas. The TRILL packet format is unchanged, but border RBridges need changed data plane processing.

facts.label: Default DBRB
facts.value: Smallest nickname, as an unsigned integer

today: RFC 9183 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2022, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits alongside the unique nickname approach of RFC 8397, and both can be used in the same TRILL campus.

sections.title: The Nickname Problem in Multilevel TRILL
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) uses 16-bit nicknames to identify its switches, called RBridges. RFC 8243 describes two approaches to multilevel TRILL. The unique nickname approach gives every switch in the whole campus a different nickname, and RFC 8397 specifies it. The aggregated nickname approach gives nicknames to areas and lets areas reuse nicknames, with border switches rewriting nickname fields.

RFC 9183 is somewhat similar to the aggregated approach, with one important difference. The nickname of an area border RBridge is used in both Level 1 (L1) and Level 2 (L2), and no extra nicknames are assigned to represent L1 areas. Instead, an L1 area is denoted by the set of nicknames of its border RBridges. Nicknames in L2 MUST be unique, while nicknames inside an L1 area can be reused in other L1 areas that use this approach.

Other approaches can still be used in other L1 areas of the same campus, such as the unique nickname approach. The TRILL packet format does not change, but data plane processing changes at border RBridges, and efficient high volume forwarding might need new forwarding hardware.
sections.eli5: Big networks are split into small areas. Instead of giving every house in the world its own number, each area may reuse numbers, and only the gates between areas need special, unique names.

sections.title: Levels, Areas and Border RBridges
sections.content:
Like IS-IS, TRILL has Level 1 for routing inside an area and Level 2 for routing between areas. Level 1 RBridges exchange routing information with others in the same L1 area, while Level 2 RBridges only form relationships with other Level 2 RBridges. An area border RBridge sits between an L1 area and Level 2.

In the RFC's example topology, RB2, RB20, RB3 and RB30 are border RBridges with nicknames 2, 20, 3 and 30. RB2 and RB20 together use the nicknames {2,20} to denote the left area, and RB3 and RB30 use {3,30} for the right area. A source S is attached to RB27 and a destination D to RB44. Those two could even have the same nickname, since the nickname is not visible outside their L1 areas.
sections.eli5: Each area has a few gates. The set of gate names is the area's name, so the area does not need a separate name of its own.

sections.title: Forwarding Unicast and Multi-destination Packets
sections.content:
For a unicast frame from S to D, RB27 learned that D is behind nickname 3 and encapsulates the frame with ingress 27 and egress 3. The border RBridges RB2 and RB20 announce in L1 that they are attached to the nicknames of all border RBridges in L2, so IS-IS routes the packet to RB2 (or RB20, if it is on the least-cost route).

When RB2 moves the packet from L1 to L2, it replaces the ingress nickname 27 with its own nickname 2. RB2 learns that S is attached to nickname 27 in area {2,20} so that return traffic works, and it SHOULD synchronize this with RB20 using the ESADI protocol. At the far side, RB3 replaces the egress nickname with RB44's nickname 44, found by looking up D. RB44 then learns that S is attached to nickname 2, one of the ingress area's nicknames.

For multi-destination packets (broadcast, multicast and unknown-unicast), distribution trees are calculated separately in each L1 area and in L2. Only one border RBridge, the Designated Border RBridge (DBRB), does the level transition for a given packet, and the other border RBridges MUST drop their copies. By default the border RBridge with the smallest nickname, treated as an unsigned integer, is the DBRB. The DBRB replaces the egress nickname with the root nickname of a distribution tree in the area the packet is entering. A border RBridge that receives a packet whose ingress nickname is a border nickname of its own area must not transition it back.
sections.eli5: When a letter passes through a gate, the gate keeper puts their own name on the return address, and on the way out writes the real house number on the front. For letters meant for everyone, only one gate keeper is allowed to pass them on, so the town does not get duplicates.

sections.title: Per-Flow Load Balancing
sections.content:
Because border RBridges rewrite nicknames anyway, they can spread traffic over several border RBridges. Using the mechanism in one of the two directions, or both, is in general necessary to load-balance traffic across L2 paths.

In the L2-to-L1 direction, a border RBridge MAY replace the packet's ingress nickname with one of the ingress area's nicknames, chosen by a pseudorandom algorithm from RFC 7357, so that return traffic is spread over multiple paths. All border RBridges of the area MUST agree on the algorithm. The source MAC address, ingress and egress area nicknames and the Data Label are candidate inputs. The destination MAC address SHOULD be excluded, otherwise the egress RBridge could see one source MAC address flip-flopping among several ingress RBridges.

In the L1-to-L2 direction, a border RBridge MAY replace the egress nickname with one of the egress area's border nicknames. By default it SHOULD choose the border RBridge with the least cost route, using the pseudorandom algorithm among equal-cost choices. The choice can be extended to non-least-cost alternatives for more load spreading, at the cost of sometimes using a longer L2 route.
sections.eli5: If a town has several gates, the gate keepers can take turns so one gate is not crowded. They pick a gate by a fair shuffle, so the same conversation always uses the same gate.

sections.title: Discovering Border RBridges
sections.content:
Discovery is triggered when a node comes up or recovers, a node goes down, or a link or node failure partitions an L1 or L2 area, or such a partition is repaired. Two new TRILL APPsub-TLVs, carried inside the TRILL GENINFO-TLV, make discovery work.

The L1-BORDER-RBRIDGE APPsub-TLV (type 256) goes in E-L1FS FS-LSP fragment zero. It has a length of 2 and carries a Sender Nickname, the nickname the originator uses as its L1 Border RBridge Nickname. Listening for it, a border RBridge discovers the other border RBridges in its area.

The L1-BORDER-RB-GROUP APPsub-TLV (type 257) goes in E-L2FS FS-LSP fragment zero. Its length is 2 * k for k nicknames, and it MUST include all L1 Border RBridge Nicknames of the area, RECOMMENDED in ascending order. If the length is not a multiple of 2, the TLV is corrupt and MUST be ignored. In L2 a border RBridge learns every group of border nicknames, and each group identifies an area. When an area is partitioned and the set changes, border RBridges that notice the change MUST flush reachability information for any nickname in the changing set.
sections.eli5: Gate keepers shout out their names so that they all know who else guards the same town, and so that the big city knows which names belong to which town.

sections.title: Multiple Areas and Compatibility
sections.content:
One border RBridge can connect several L1 areas. It SHOULD use a single area nickname for all of them, to minimize nickname use and the number of nicknames advertised in L2, although it might need more nicknames if it is the root of several distribution trees. Since the areas form one layer 2 network, duplicate {MAC, Data Label} pairs across areas SHOULD NOT occur. For unicast, such a border RBridge uses its MAC table to find the right outgoing area, and for multicast it floods only into the areas where it is the DBRB, never back into the originating area.

All Level 2 RBridges MUST support E-L2FS, and area border RBridges MUST support both E-L1FS and E-L2FS. RBridges that lack this cannot be border RBridges but can be ordinary RBridges inside an L1 area. A border RBridge configured for single nickname multilevel MUST also support the unique nickname approach of RFC 8397, and it MUST fall back to unique nickname behavior for an area if another border RBridge of that area supports only unique nicknames. Operators SHOULD be notified when this fallback happens.
sections.eli5: A gate keeper who guards several towns uses just one name for all of them. If a neighbor gate keeper cannot play by the new rules, everyone in that town goes back to the older, simpler rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new APPsub-TLVs travel in IS-IS PDUs, whose authenticity can be enforced with regular IS-IS security mechanisms. Malicious devices could fake the TLVs to attract data packets, interfere with multilevel TRILL, or induce excessive state in switches. For that reason RBridges SHOULD be configured to use the IS-IS Authentication TLV (10) so forged PDUs are discarded.

Reusing nicknames between areas also raises the chance that a data packet reaches the wrong egress RBridge if areas are unexpectedly merged, compared with a scheme where nicknames are unique. In many cases the data would be discarded at that egress RBridge because it would not match a known end station Data Label and MAC address.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be a gate keeper and steal letters, so the gate keepers should check each other's ID badges.
